newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha resigns, leaving Albania in chaos.
newsitem.headline: Berisha resigns, leaving Albania in chaos.

text.p: Sali Berisha, who resigned as Albanian president on Wednesday to join the parliamentary opposition after his party's election defeat, leaves to his successor a country in social and economic chaos.

The former heart surgeon and communist was initially praised in the West for a rapid introduction of market reforms but the glow faded last year as he resorted to authoritarianism and failed to check the spread of shady pyramid investment schemes.

"I think that Albanians in these five years based on their free initiative did more for themselves and their families than at any time before, and that they had...the greatest international solidarity," he said in his resignation letter.

"The financial pyramid scheme crisis, of course a negative phenomenon of our governing, was exploited as a pretext by the former Albanian communists to organise the armed communist rebellion," Berisha said.

The collapse of five such funds early this year unleashed a wave of violence which has killed more than 1,500 people. A million looted weapons are thought to be in private hands and gangster-ridden anarchy plagues the south of Albania.
Parliament elected the 55-year-old Berisha to a second five-year term in March a day after the imposition of a nationwide state of emergency.
Many people expected him to go into exile after the Balkan nation came to the brink of anarchy, but he stayed to create a government of national unity led by his Socialist rivals.
But after the Democrats' defeat in June 29 parliamentary elections he said he would not cohabit with a Socialist government. He will sit in parliament as an opposition deputy.
Berisha was the darling of the West in the early 1990s, respected for anchoring stability in Albania while the war in Bosnia threatened to ignite the Balkan tinderbox.

When he took power in April 1992, Sarajevo was about to suffer one of the bloodiest assaults on a European city since World War Two and hundreds of thousands of refugees were on the move from former Yugoslavia, which shared a border with Albania.

Berisha, a former university cardiologist, repeatedly urged his people to remain calm while ethnic Albanians over the border in Kosovo, in southern Yugoslavia, came under increasing threat from Serbian nationalists in Belgrade.

Berisha won the confidence of foreign governments and international lending institutions with his economic reform plans. Speaking fluent English and French, he seemed every bit the leader of a new Albania, eager to embrace Western values and to push for closer ties with NATO and the European Union.
The United States turned the once-Stalinist state into its closest ally in the region, sending military advisers and aid.
Berisha co-founded the Democratic Party in December 1990 after a student uprising forced communist President Ramiz Alia to allow political parties and free elections.
The communist system had permitted him to study in France and he was a member of the medical team that administered to high-ranking leaders.
The Democrats selected him to lead the party in 1991 before going on to win the 1992 general election by a landslide.
Berisha rode a wave of popularity until a referendum in 1994 rejected a draft constitution which would have given more power to the president.

Opposition parties say that was when the mood began to change. Amnesty International criticised the jailing of Socialist Party leader Fatos Nano, Berisha's main rival, on corruption charges. Washington did the same when supreme court chief Zef Brozi was sacked after declaring that Nano was innocent.
The May 1996 general election was widely criticised by foreign observers and boycotted by the main opposition parties who alleged voter intimidation and ballot-box stuffing.
This severely damaged Berisha's international standing and relations with Washington, which called for fresh elections at the earlier possible date, quickly cooled.
Berisha's defiant resignation letter contended that the new parliament marked "the return to power of the last communist nomenklatura".
"The hours to come will give the possibility to all Albanians coldbloodedly to consider once again the five years of democracy and the five months of rebellion," he said.
